Podiatry · published research

Diabetic foot ulcer

Evidence overview

Research on diabetic foot ulcers

Summary of the Evidence

Research on diabetic foot ulcers includes clinical studies, reviews, protocols, and editorials. Several controlled trials report reductions in ulcer area with selected red or near-infrared PBM protocols, and some also report complete healing. Findings vary across protocols and outcomes.

Human and clinical evidence

In an 80-participant randomized, placebo-controlled dose-response trial, all groups received standard wound care and the active groups received 904-nm PBM at different energy densities. At 10 weeks, the 10 J/cm² group was the only dose group reported as significantly different from placebo for ulcer-area reduction; 60% of ulcers in that group achieved complete healing. This is a positive result for that tested regimen (Cardoso et al. 2024).

A double-blind pilot in 20 people with severe, osteomyelitis-associated ulcers compared at-home 808-nm PBM plus standard care with sham plus standard care. More than 90% closure was reported for 7/10 active-treatment participants and 1/10 sham participants, alongside a greater reduction in ulcer area in the active group. The sample was small, but the result is notable in this high-severity population (Haze et al. 2022).

Other randomized comparisons also report area reductions with particular protocols. A 660-nm, 3 J/cm² regimen added to conventional care reduced ulcer area by 37% on average over two weeks, versus 15% with conventional care alone (Mathur et al. 2017). A sham-controlled study of grade-II ulcers reported greater area reduction after 904-nm PBM at 2 J/cm² over four weeks (Torkaman et al. 2024). In an earlier small trial, 58.3% of active-treated ulcers had healed completely by day 90, compared with one ulcer in the very-low-output sham group; the report included 23 ulcers in 14 people (Minatel et al. 2009).

Not every comparison separates active regimens. In a 2025 dose-response study, all groups received PBM alongside wound care; no significant difference in area reduction was found between the tested 660-nm doses and 904-nm regimen at five or ten weeks. This was a comparison among active protocols, not a PBM-versus-no-PBM test (Miranda et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly focused on diabetic foot ulcers was included among the records reviewed.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The clinical reports include red 660-nm and near-infrared 808- and 904-nm protocols, as well as combined red/near-infrared LED treatments. Energy density, session frequency, ulcer severity, comparators, follow-up, and accompanying wound care differ. Most studies test PBM as an addition to standard wound care, so the evidence supports protocol-specific findings rather than one established dose schedule.

Interpretation

The literature includes positive randomized findings for ulcer-area reduction and, in selected studies, complete closure. The size and certainty of benefit vary by protocol and outcome. Some trials found no clear difference between PBM protocols. Others found better outcomes with PBM than with sham treatment or usual care alone.

Larger trials using clearly described protocols and reporting both area change and complete healing over time would help establish which regimens benefit which ulcers.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term ulcer-area reduction with selected protocolsLow for complete closure and time to healing across protocols
Publications and records71 database records

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several controlled trials report short-term ulcer-area reductions with selected red or near-infrared protocols, and some report complete closure.

Confidence remains limited by small samples, varied ulcer severity, regimens, comparators, and endpoints. Larger trials should predefine complete healing and time to closure alongside area change.
